observation.visible_scene: A close view of a light patch projected onto a pale wall/surface. A diagonal metal rod with a blue anodized collar lies at the right, and a mottled marble floor is partly visible at the upper right in the earliest frames. The projected spot sits left-of-center throughout.
visible_changes: The projected spot begins as an overexposed white blob with only a faint blue fringe on its right; over the sequence it resolves into a vertical rainbow pattern with distinct bands (red, yellow/orange, green, cyan, blue, violet) while a diffuse blue tail continues to extend to the right.

The overall illumination of the surface drops steadily: the wall goes from bright white in the first frames to mid-gray and then dark gray by the end, which makes the spectrum appear more saturated and contrasted.

The metal rod and the marble-floor edge at the right gradually leave the frame (the rod shrinks to a thin dark diagonal at the bottom-right corner), indicating relative motion between the camera and the scene elements.

The spectrum patch itself stays roughly in the same left-of-center position with only minor drift, so the dominant change is in its internal color structure and the global brightness rather than large translation of the spot.
outside_clip_unknowns: What optical element or source produces the projection, and whether the color resolution is caused by a moving element, a changing aperture, or simply by the exposure/ambient light dropping.
The state before t=0 and the outcome after t=3.33 s; the segment is a mid-action crop.
Whether the rod/floor shift is camera pan/tilt or physical movement of the rod.
uncertain_details: The exact cause of the darkening and of the spectrum 'appearing' (exposure change vs. optical change) cannot be determined from the frames.
The relative motion of the rod versus the wall boundary is ambiguous; it could be camera movement, object movement, or both.
Band boundaries are soft and the colors blur, so the precise spectral ordering/edges are approximate.
